questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Matter wavelength of a slow electron
questions.learningObjective: Relate the matter wavelength of a slow particle to its momentum.
questions.stem: The apiary workshop log records a cathode ray tube in which electrons drifted at 200 m/s for a school demonstration. What matter wavelength should the log quote for such an electron?

options.text: 3.64 x 10^-6 m, found by dividing Planck's constant by the electron's momentum.
1.26 x 10^-6 m, found by dividing the electron's mass by the speed of light.
options.misconception: divides the mass by c instead of using p = mv

options.text: 9.11 x 10^-31 m, found by using the electron mass as though it were a wavelength.
options.misconception: confuses the electron mass with a wavelength

options.text: 1.60 x 10^-19 m, found by using the electron charge as though it were a wavelength.
options.misconception: confuses the electron charge with a wavelength

questions.explanation: Every moving object carries a matter wave with wavelength λ = h/p = h/(mv), and a slow electron has a small momentum, so its wavelength is large. Using the mass or the charge as a wavelength describes nothing physical.
questions.hint: Matter wavelength equals h over momentum.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Matter wavelength of a macroscopic object
questions.learningObjective: Estimate the matter wavelength of an everyday moving object.
questions.stem: A logbook line records a jar of honey weighing 2.0 kg being slid across a bench at a steady 0.50 m/s. What matter wavelength belongs to that jar?

options.misconception: uses the mass alone and ignores the speed

options.text: 6.63 x 10^-34 m, from dividing Planck's constant by a momentum of 1.0 kg m/s.
3.31 x 10^-34 m, from dividing Planck's constant by a momentum of 2.0 kg m/s.
options.misconception: halves the momentum by using the mass alone

options.text: 1.33 x 10^-33 m, from dividing the jar's mass by its speed.
options.misconception: divides mass by speed to get a momentum

questions.hint: Find the momentum first, then divide h by it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Energy of a hydrogen level
questions.learningObjective: Find the energy of a hydrogen level from the quantum number.
questions.stem: The workshop's hydrogen discharge lamp is used to attract moths to a trap beside the hives. Explain how you would find the energy of the n = 3 level of the hydrogen in that lamp.

answer.exemplar: Hydrogen levels are quantised and follow E_n = −13.6 eV divided by n squared, with the zero of energy at an ionised electron at rest. For n = 3 this gives E_3 = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV, measured relative to that reference, so the level lies 1.51 eV below a free electron. Every photon leaving the lamp carries exactly the energy difference between two such levels.

questions.explanation: Bound hydrogen levels follow E_n = −13.6/n² eV, so the n = 3 level sits at −1.51 eV relative to a free electron at infinity. The negative sign marks a bound state, not a negative energy.
questions.hint: Use the hydrogen level energy formula.

options.misconception: confuses a Balmer line with a Lyman transition

options.text: An electron rising from n = 2 to n = 3 by absorbing a red Balmer photon.
options.misconception: describes an upward transition as a line source

options.text: An electron dropping from n = 3 to n = 1, which produces a line in the Lyman series.
options.misconception: mixes a Balmer line with a Lyman transition

options.text: An electron dropping from n = 3 to n = 2, releasing the red line of the Balmer series.

questions.explanation: Balmer lines are the transitions that end on n = 2, and the longest and strongest of them, 656.3 nm, is the n = 3 to n = 2 drop. Absorption lines in the Sun's spectrum are made by the same transitions seen in reverse.
questions.hint: Balmer lines all end on the level n = 2.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Momentum spread from a position accuracy
questions.learningObjective: Explain the momentum uncertainty implied by a precise position.
questions.stem: A high-speed camera in the apiary shed tracks a single pollen grain and localises it to 2.0 x 10^-12 m. Explain what the uncertainty principle says about the grain's momentum.

answer.exemplar: The uncertainty relation ties the position accuracy Δx to the momentum spread by Δp >= ħ/(2Δx) = 1.055 x 10^-34/(4.0 x 10^-12) = 2.64 x 10^-23 kg m/s for a grain localised that tightly. Sharpening the image, for instance by shortening the exposure, shrinks Δx and therefore enlarges the range of momenta the grain could be carrying. The two quantities cannot both be sharply defined at once.

questions.explanation: A precise position fixes a narrow Δx, and the relation Δp >= ħ/(2Δx) then forces a broad momentum spread. Improving the image in one direction inevitably blurs the other.
questions.hint: Position accuracy and momentum spread trade off.

options.text: The speed spread is unaffected, because the position accuracy sets the momentum only.

The speed spread becomes zero, since an exact position determines the velocity completely.

questions.explanation: Tightening Δx widens Δp by the uncertainty relation, and since Δv = Δp/m for a particle of fixed mass, the speed spread widens too. A position measurement never fixes a velocity completely.
questions.hint: A tighter position forces a wider momentum spread.

questions.stem: A logbook entry describes a swarm of bees hovering outside the hive, each bee moving slowly at a few metres per second. Explain what the matter wave idea predicts for such bees.

answer.exemplar: Every body with momentum carries a wave of wavelength λ = h/p = h/(mv). A bee of mass about 1.0 x 10^-4 kg flying at 5.0 m/s has a momentum of 5.0 x 10^-4 kg m/s, so its matter wavelength is only 1.3 x 10^-30 m. questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Energy of a hydrogen level
questions.learningObjective: Explain why hydrogen lines crowd together towards the ultraviolet.
questions.stem: A page of the logbook asks why the hydrogen lines emitted by the workshop lamp crowd closer together as they approach the ultraviolet. Explain the pattern in terms of level energies.

answer.exemplar: The bound levels of hydrogen are E_n = −13.6/n² eV, so the energy needed to lift an electron from n to n + 1 shrinks rapidly as n grows: 10.2 eV from n = 1, then 1.89 eV, then 0.66 eV, and so on. A photon carrying the difference between two levels therefore has a smaller energy for the higher pairs, and the emitted lines bunch up towards the ultraviolet where the level spacing becomes tiny.

questions.explanation: Hydrogen levels crowd toward zero energy as n rises, so the energy differences between neighbouring levels shrink. The emitted photon energies shrink with them, and smaller energies mean shorter wavelengths.
questions.hint: The spacing between high levels gets smaller.

answer.exemplar: Solving the Schrödinger equation for hydrogen with a Coulomb potential gives bound levels E_n = −13.6 eV divided by n squared, where n is a positive whole number and the zero of energy is taken at an ionised electron. questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Matter wavelength of a slow electron
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the matter wavelength from a stated momentum.
questions.stem: A log entry gives the momentum of a slow electron in the workshop tube as 2.0 x 10^-29 kg m/s. What is its matter wavelength, in units of 10^-5 m?
questions.explanation: The matter wavelength is λ = h/p = 6.626 x 10^-34/2.0 x 10^-29 = 3.31 x 10^-5 m, that is 33 microns. Slow electrons therefore carry wavelengths of the size of fine dust.
questions.hint: Divide Planck's constant by the momentum.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Matter wavelength of a macroscopic object
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the matter wavelength of a moving crate.
questions.stem: A logbook entry notes a 2.0 kg honey crate being carried at 1.5 m/s across the apiary yard. What is the matter wavelength of the crate, in units of 10^-34 m?
questions.explanation: The momentum is mv = 2.0 x 1.5 = 3.0 kg m/s, so λ = h/p = 2.21 x 10^-34 m. Everyday masses and speeds give wavelengths far too small to observe.
questions.hint: Multiply mass by speed to get the momentum.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Matter wavelength of an accelerated electron
questions.learningObjective: Compare matter wavelengths at two different accelerating voltages.
questions.stem: A worksheet question asks how the matter wavelength of the demonstration electrons changes when the tube voltage is raised from 100 V to 400 V. Which two-stage reasoning answers it?

options.text: Divide the two voltages to get a ratio, then square it to obtain the wavelength ratio.
options.misconception: squares a voltage ratio to get a wavelength ratio

options.text: Multiply the two voltages to get a total energy, then take its square root for the wavelength.
options.misconception: adds energies by multiplying voltages

options.text: Convert each voltage into an energy with E = eV, then use λ = h/sqrt(2mE) for each.
Convert each voltage into a wavelength with c = fλ, then compare the two wavelengths.
options.misconception: misuses the light wave relation on electrons

questions.explanation: At 100 V the electrons have a wavelength near 1.23 x 10^-10 m and at 400 V near 6.13 x 10^-11 m, since λ scales as one over the square root of the energy. The light relation c = fλ has no place here.
questions.hint: Voltage to energy, then the de Broglie formula.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Momentum spread from a position accuracy
questions.learningObjective: Explain the position and momentum trade-off for an everyday object.
questions.stem: A final logbook page asks how far the idea of a matter wave is from everyday beekeeping. Explain what the uncertainty principle says about measuring a bee precisely.

answer.exemplar: The uncertainty relation Δp >= ħ/(2Δx) applies to any body, however ordinary. A bee of mass 1.0 x 10^-4 kg tracked to within 1.0 x 10^-5 m has a momentum spread of at least 5.27 x 10^-30 kg m/s, and to 1.0 x 10^-9 m still at least 5.27 x 10^-26 kg m/s. Tightening the position in the film or the camera therefore blurs the momentum, and no amount of optical cleverness can measure a bee's position and momentum sharply at the same time.

questions.explanation: The same trade-off between position and momentum applies to a bee as to an electron, so even the best tracking leaves the momentum uncertain. Sharper images widen the momentum spread rather than narrowing it.
questions.hint: Position accuracy and momentum spread trade off.
